transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-09
Start: 14:30 PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jesse Huang (Redwood SE), Nina Park (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Polaris CTO), Aaron Lee (ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Head Infra), Priya Desai (Product)

Auto-summary (note: auto gen): Polaris is building a customer-facing conversational assistant with multi-turn context, streaming UI, and need for sub-400ms p95 on short prompts. Looking at Redwood hosted for fast start, dedicated for predictable throughput, private/VPC for data residency. Critical items: benchmarking token/sec, understanding batching/kv cache behavior, and validating SSO/KMS + audit logs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Samir here from Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Maya: Hi, Maya Thompson, CTO at Polaris.
[00:07] Aaron: Aaron Lee, ML eng.
[00:09] Liam: Liam O'Connor, infra.
[00:11] Priya: Priya, product.
[00:12] Samir: Great. Jesse and Nina from our SE team are on — Jesse will probably walk through the latency/throughput stuff.
[00:17] Jesse: Yep, thanks. So Polaris, we saw in your note you're targeting p95 numbers in the 200–400ms range for short interactive prompts, and heavier long-form batches for nightly generation. Is that right?
[00:25] Maya: Yeah that's correct. For the chat UI we want p95 under 350ms ideally, for prompts under ~400 tokens. We also want streaming so the UI feels snappy. For batch we care more about tokens/sec and cost — we're looking at something like 2000–3000 tokens/sec for large jobs.
[00:39] Jesse: Okay, and concurrency — how many concurrent users or streams in peak?
[00:43] Maya: Peak concurrent streams probably around 150–250. But bursts could go up to 400 for promotions.
[00:49] Aaron: To add, the distribution is heavy tail — most requests are short, 30–60 tokens, but we have a 5–10% tail of long 1k–4k prompts.
[00:59] Nina: That helps. So two main buckets: low-latency interactive with streaming and high-throughput batch. We'll discuss hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs.
[01:08] Liam: From infra/security perspective we're leaning private/VPC but open to a hosted pilot if the data classification permits. We need SSO, audit logs, and bring-your-own-KMS for production.
[01:17] Jesse: All standard. Redwood Private supports VPC deployments and customer KMS integrations. Hosted can be used for pilot — with strict contract terms — but for production sounds like Dedicated or Private makes sense.
[01:27] Maya: What do you typically see for p95 on hosted for short prompts on your verified models?
[01:32] Jesse: For the models we "verify" in our catalog, p95 for 50–100 token prompts typically sits between 120–320ms on our hosted service depending on model size and quantization. On Dedicated we can push that lower and get more predictable tails because of reserved GPUs, and Private gives you full control over networking and KMS.
[01:48] Aaron: How much of that is due to batching and how much is pure model latency?
[01:52] Jesse: Good question. It's a mix — model decoding plus overheads. Continuous batching helps overall throughput but introduces queuing latency. For interactive streaming we bias towards smaller batches and prefix/KV cache hits to reduce end-to-end latency. We also use sequence-length aware kernel selection to avoid worst-case slowdowns.
[02:10] Maya: Can you explain KV cache behavior? We use a lot of multi-turn context, want to avoid re-encoding.
[02:15] Nina: Yeah, KV cache (sometimes transcribed as K V cache) keeps keys/values across tokens so repeated prefixes are fast. For multi-turn chat we keep session KV entries in memory; this reduces compute on the prefix by ~30–60% depending on prompt reuse. There's also an LRU cache for long-tail sessions.
[02:31] Aaron: Is the KV cache shared across instances or per-GPU?
[02:35] Jesse: Per-inference-worker, but the routing layer tries to keep affinity for warm sessions to the same worker when possible. In Dedicated you can tune that for stronger session stickiness.
[02:44] Liam: On the networking side, for VPC peering what throughput do you need? Any ports or protocols specifics?
[02:50] Samir: We can do VPC peering or private link; typically we recommend peering with minimum 10 Gbps for high-throughput workloads. We'll share a network guide.
[02:58] Priya: Back to streaming — how do you handle partial tokens? We want very low time-to-first-byte for UI.
[03:04] Jesse: We stream token deltas immediately; time-to-first-byte depends mostly on initial decoding and model cold start. Warm workers with KV cache and pre-warmed kernels get first byte under 80–120ms for short prompts on dedicated hardware.
[03:17] Maya: You mentioned cold starts — how often do those happen on hosted?
[03:21] Nina: On hosted, scaling to zero can introduce cold starts. For production we provision minimum warm capacity and use burst capacity; Dedicated avoids multi-tenant cold starts entirely.
[03:30] Aaron: What about benchmarking — token/sec. If we run a microbenchmark, what config should we include?
[03:35] Jesse: For a useful token/sec benchmark include: model variant (fp16/int8), sequence lengths distribution, batch sizes you expect, concurrency pattern, and whether you want streaming or whole-output. We'll send a template. Expected ranges: on 4xA100 class Dedicated with int8 and batching you might see ~2500–5000 tokens/sec depending on model and batch. On CPU or smaller GPUs it's lower.
[03:56] Maya: For our initial pilot we'll use a 2B-7B style open model, probably quantized. Does Redwood support mixed-precision and quantization out of the box?
[04:04] Jesse: Yes — we have quantization profiles and kernel paths that target int8/q4 variants. We expose recommended profiles in the console and can suggest quantization versus accuracy tradeoffs.
[04:13] Aaron: Do you have real examples of p95 pre/post quantization?
[04:17] Jesse: Quick example: a 7B model quantized to q4 on Dedicated might reduce latency by ~15–25% with negligible loss on many prompts. We'll include a few reference numbers in the benchmark template.
[04:29] Maya: If we want to maintain p95 <350ms for 95% of short prompts, is that realistic with a quantized 7B on Dedicated under 200 concurrency?
[04:38] Jesse: Yes, with correct batching and KV cache affinity you can hit that. Important to tune batching window and serve hot sessions on pre-warmed workers. If you expect spikes to 400 concurrent streams, then burst capacity or autoscaling needs to be planned — Dedicated gives you reserved baseline + burst pools.
[04:55] Liam: For autoscaling, how fast can you scale up GPUs? Minutes? Seconds?
[04:59] Nina: Typically minutes — instance spin-up is minutes. For fast bursts we recommend a warm burst pool or pre-warmed containers. We can also do predictive scaling based on schedules.
[05:09] Aaron: Any chance to see packet or telemetry for token/sec during a run? We need per-route token/sec and per-token cost telemetry.
[05:15] Samir: Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and traces. We'll share screenshots.
[05:23] Maya: Security — SOC 2, KMS, audit logs, SSO. Anything we should expect?
[05:27] Samir: We're SOC 2 compliant, can integrate with customer KMS, and provide audit logging and RBAC. For Private we can offer an on-prem package and stricter data residency.
[05:36] Priya: Any common gotchas?
[05:38] Jesse: Watch out for tail latency on long-token requests; they can block worker throughput if not isolated. Recommended: route long-form batch to dedicated endpoints and reserve workers for interactive short requests. Also watch for tokenization differences across model variants — that affects tokens/sec estimates.
[05:53] Maya: Can you run a short benchmark on our sample prompts and return results?
[05:56] Samir: Absolutely — best path is you send the 200 sample prompts + concurrency pattern, we run a 1-day microbenchmark on a configured Dedicated instance and share raw token/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and suggestions.
[06:08] Aaron: Sounds good.
[06:09] Samir: Quick recap — action items: Samir sends pricing and security pack, Jesse preps batch/quant configs and benchmark template, Polaris provides samples and confirms VPC peering window. We'll aim to schedule Dedicated sizing call next week.
[06:22] Maya: Thanks, that's helpful.
[06:24] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the docs and booking link.
[06:28] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional words mis-transcribed (e.g., K V cache vs KV cache), some speaker labels simplified.
